title: Should @Transactional go on the class, the implementation, or the interface? Explain how JDK dynamic proxies differ from CGLIB proxies and why you should always put @Transactional on the implementation.
shortTitle: @Transactional on class vs interface: JDK proxy vs CGLIB?
keyPoints: Spring implements @Transactional through an AOP proxy that wraps the bean and intercepts method calls
JDK dynamic proxy implements the bean's interfaces and reads annotations from interface methods
CGLIB proxy generates a subclass of the concrete class and reads annotations from the implementation
Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB (proxyTargetClass = true) since Spring 5 and Spring Boot 2
@Transactional on an interface may be silently ignored under CGLIB; always annotate the implementation
CGLIB requires the class and transactional methods to be non-final; private methods are not proxied

s1_definition.oneliner: Always put @Transactional on the implementation class, not the interface, because Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB proxies which subclass the concrete class and may not see annotations on interfaces.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **AOP Proxy** – Spring wraps the bean in a proxy that intercepts method calls and manages the transaction lifecycle (begin, commit, rollback).
- **JDK Dynamic Proxy** – created by `java.lang.reflect.Proxy`; works only when the bean implements an interface; reads annotations from the interface methods.
- **CGLIB Proxy** – generates a subclass of the concrete class at runtime; does not require an interface; reads annotations from the implementation class.
- **Spring Boot default** – since Spring 5 and Spring Boot 2, `proxyTargetClass = true` is the default, meaning CGLIB is used even when interfaces are present.
- **Recommendation** – always annotate the implementation so the annotation works under both proxy types; keep classes and transactional methods non-final and public.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the proxy is a security guard standing in front of the real clerk. With a JDK proxy, the guard reads the rulebook posted on the public counter (the interface). With a CGLIB proxy, the guard is a stand-in wearing the clerk's uniform (a subclass) who reads the rules from the clerk's own notebook (the implementation). Spring Boot hires the uniform-wearing stand-in by default, so the transaction rule must be in the clerk's notebook or it gets ignored.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  JDK Dynamic Proxy                      CGLIB Proxy (Spring Boot default)
  ──────────────────                      ──────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────┐                   ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │  Proxy (JDK)     │                   │  Proxy (CGLIB subclass)      │
  │  implements:     │                   │  extends:                     │
  │  TransferService │                   │  TransferServiceImpl          │
  │  (interface)     │                   │  (concrete class)             │
  │                  │                   │                               │
  │  Reads @TX from  │                   │  Reads @TX from               │
  │  INTERFACE       │                   │  IMPLEMENTATION               │
  └────────┬─────────┘                   └──────────────┬───────────────┘
           │                                             │
           ▼                                             ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐                   ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │  TransferService │                   │  TransferServiceImpl          │
  │  Impl (target)   │                   │  (target, same class)         │
  └──────────────────┘                   └──────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Spring implements @Transactional through an AOP proxy that wraps the bean. There are two kinds of proxy: JDK dynamic proxy, which implements the bean's interfaces and reads annotations from interface methods, and CGLIB proxy, which generates a subclass of the concrete class and reads annotations from the implementation. Since Spring 5 and Spring Boot 2, CGLIB is the default (proxyTargetClass = true), even when the bean has an interface.

This default is why annotation placement matters. At National Bank of India, a developer once put @Transactional on the TransferService interface and left the TransferServiceImpl bare. Because Spring Boot used CGLIB, the annotation was silently ignored, no transaction started, and a failing transfer left money half-moved between Rajesh's account SAV2001 and Priya's account SAV3002. The fix is to always put @Transactional on the implementation class or its methods, keeping the interface clean.

CGLIB has a few additional rules. The class must not be final (cannot subclass), transactional methods must not be final (cannot override), and private methods are never proxied. In Kotlin, where classes are final by default, use the kotlin-spring compiler plugin which automatically opens annotated classes. The self-invocation rule applies under both proxy types: calling a transactional method on this bypasses the proxy.

Remember one sentence: always put @Transactional on the implementation, not the interface, because Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB proxies which read annotations from the concrete class, not the interface.
